title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text: 17.1 The idea behind it
crumbs: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum

title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text:
Schema-aware processing. Once Spark knows the columns and types, it can optimise your query (the Catalyst optimiser): push filters before joins, read only the needed columns, generate efficient JVM code. The same idea underlies SQL databases (MySQL lab), now applied to distributed files.
Declarative over imperative. With RDDs you say how (call this lambda on every element); with DataFrames you say what (filter, group, aggregate) and Spark decides how. Everything you write in Python is a plan; execution stays in the JVM unless you force Python code in with UDFs.
Physics analysis is an ETL pipeline: Extract (read raw events), Transform (select, flatten, compute features), Load/reduce (histograms). The same shape appears in industry pipelines.
crumbs: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum

title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text:
17.2 Why DataFrames
An RDD is a distributed list of arbitrary Python objects: Spark cannot see inside them, so it cannot optimise anything. A DataFrame is a distributed table: named columns with types (a schema). Knowing the structure lets Spark plan the query (the Catalyst optimiser), store data column-wise, and run most operations inside the JVM without touching Python. Underneath, it is still partitions of an RDD (df.rdd), so everything from Spark 1 about laziness, partitions, collect and persist still applies.
The session is the same as before, with two extra settings that switch on Apache Arrow for moving data between the JVM and Python (used by toPandas() and pandas UDFs):
.config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
.config("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.fallback.enabled", "false")
crumbs: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum

title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text:
17.3 Creating DataFrames








From
How
Schema




list of Row(a=1, b=2., …)
spark.createDataFrame([...])
inferred from the Rows


list of tuples
spark.createDataFrame([...], schema='a long, b double, …')
given explicitly


a pandas DataFrame
spark.createDataFrame(pandas_df)
from pandas dtypes


files
spark.read.format('json').load(path)
inferred or given


an RDD of Rows
rdd.toDF()
inferred



df.show() prints rows (an action); df.printSchema() prints the structure (no job).
The toDF() route is the general escape hatch: when the file format is not supported natively, parse it with RDD code (as in Spark 1), produce Row objects, and convert.
pyspark.pandas offers a near-identical pandas API on top of Spark (ps.DataFrame(...)). It is handy for porting pandas code, but not everything is implemented, and some pandas habits are expensive when distributed. For example, there is no natural row order across partitions, and enforcing one means a full sort. The lab uses the regular PySpark API.
crumbs: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum

title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text:
17.4 The analysis: dimuon invariant mass
The dataset is a small sample of CMS 2010 events (CERN Open Data), already converted to JSON, plus matching Monte Carlo simulation. Each record has nMuon, sample ("data" or "mc") and a nested array Muons, where each muon has E, px, py, pz, charge.

The physics: when a particle decays into two muons of opposite charge, the invariant mass of the pair, \(M = \sqrt{E^2 - |\vec p|^2}\) with \(E, \vec p\) summed over both muons, peaks at the parent’s mass. In this range that means the Z boson at ~91 GeV.

17.4.1 Step 0: load and inspect
df = spark.read.option("inferTimestamp", "false").option("prefersDecimal", "false") \
          .format('json').load('/mapd-workspace/datasets/lecture2/dimuon/*.json')
df.printSchema()
df.groupBy('sample').count().show()
Reading is lazy too: Spark only samples the files to infer the schema. Look at the schema closely: Muons is array<struct<...>>, so the data is not flat, and dealing with that is half the exercise.
Every later action would re-read the JSON from disk, so the solution caches it:
df = df.persist()   # NOT in place: without the assignment df still reads from files
df.count()          # trigger it


17.4.2 Step 1: aggregate on the cluster, plot locally
Histogram of muons per event, data vs MC:
num_muons = df.groupBy('sample', 'nMuon').count().sort('nMuon').toPandas()
This is the pattern for the whole lab: the cluster does the heavy aggregation, and only a small table comes back (toPandas(), which is fast thanks to Arrow) for matplotlib. toPandas() has the same danger as collect(): never call it on the raw dataset.


17.4.3 Step 2: filter and flatten
Keep events with exactly two muons. These are equivalent, so use whichever reads best:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
df[df['nMuon'] == 2]
df.where(col('nMuon') == 2)          # where == filter
df.filter("nMuon == 2")              # SQL expression string

df.createOrReplaceTempView("dimuon_df_table")
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM dimuon_df_table WHERE nMuon = 2")   # plain SQL
All four produce the same plan, because the optimiser sees through the syntax.
Flattening turns the nested array into ordinary columns:
dimuon_flat = (
    dimuon_df.select(col('sample'), col('nMuon'), col('Muons')[0], col('Muons')[1])
    .withColumn('E1',  col('Muons[0].E'))   .withColumn('px1', col('Muons[0].px'))
    .withColumn('py1', col('Muons[0].py'))  .withColumn('pz1', col('Muons[0].pz'))
    .withColumn('c1',  col('Muons[0].charge'))
    # ... same for muon 2 ...
    .drop('Muons[0]', 'Muons[1]')
)
select chooses columns, withColumn(name, expr) adds or replaces one, and drop removes them. Each returns a new DataFrame, since DataFrames are immutable.


17.4.4 Step 3: new features (native functions vs UDFs)
Opposite charge, then the four-momentum of the pair and its mass, using column expressions:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sqrt
dimuon_flat = (dimuon_flat.where(col('c1') != col('c2'))
    .withColumn('E',  col('E1')  + col('E2'))
    .withColumn('px', col('px1') + col('px2'))   # ... py, pz
    .withColumn('M',  sqrt(col('E')**2 - (col('px')**2 + col('py')**2 + col('pz')**2))))
The notebook then computes the same mass in two other ways, to compare the cost:








Way
Code
What runs where




native column functions
sqrt(col(...) ...)
entirely in the JVM, optimised, so fastest


Python UDF
@udf('float') def m(E, px, py, pz): return math.sqrt(...)
rows are shipped one by one to a Python process and back, so slowest


pandas UDF
@pandas_udf('float') def m(E: pd.Series, ...) -> pd.Series: return np.sqrt(...)
whole batches go to Python via Arrow and are processed vectorised with numpy, a good middle ground



The rule: use a native function if one exists, a pandas UDF if you need custom Python, and a plain UDF only as a last resort. The same comparison is repeated for an aggregation (mean energy per sample): native groupBy('sample').mean() vs groupBy('sample').agg(mean_udf(col('E'))) with a pandas UDF that returns a scalar.


17.4.5 Step 4: rediscover the Z boson
The histogram is computed on the cluster with the RDD histogram from Spark 1, so only bin counts travel:
bins, counts = dimuon_flat.where(col('sample') == 'data').select('M') \
                          .rdd.map(lambda r: r.M) \
                          .histogram(list(np.arange(0, 150, 4)))
Repeat for mc, then plot data as points with \(\sqrt{N}\) error bars over the simulation as a filled histogram. The full range (log scale) shows several resonances; zooming into 70–115 GeV with 0.5 GeV bins shows the Z peak and where the simulation disagrees with data.
A selection to improve agreement. The transverse momentum of the pair, \(p_T = \sqrt{(p_{x1}+p_{x2})^2 + (p_{y1}+p_{y2})^2}\), computed with a pandas UDF (np.hypot), then a boolean column with when/otherwise, the DataFrame version of an if/else:
from pyspark.sql.functions import when
dimuon_flat = dimuon_flat.withColumn("pT", candidate_pt(col('px1'), col('py1'), col('px2'), col('py2'))) \
                         .withColumn("highpt", when(col('pT') > 30, True).otherwise(False))
Plotting low-\(p_T\) and high-\(p_T\) candidates side by side shows how the selection changes the background and the data–MC agreement.






In the solutions, the pandas_udf candidate_pt declares its parameters as (px1, px2, py1, py2) but is called with (px1, py1, px2, py2). Arguments are matched by position, so inside the function px2 is actually py1. Write the signature in the same order you call it.
crumbs: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum

title: 17  Lab: Spark 2, DataFrames and the dimuon spectrum
text:
17.5 On a real cluster

File formats matter more than code. JSON is convenient but slow (text, parsed row by row, schema inferred). Real pipelines convert once to Parquet: columnar, compressed, with the schema stored inside, so a query reading 2 of 50 columns reads ~4% of the data. df.write.parquet("s3a://bucket/dimuon/", partitionBy=["sample"]) then spark.read.parquet(...).
Partitioned storage (partitionBy) lets Spark skip whole directories when you filter on that column (partition pruning).
spark.sql(...) and the DataFrame API are interchangeable, so data teams often expose tables to SQL users through a metastore (Hive, Unity Catalog) on top of the same files.
UDF cost scales with data: a Python UDF that is “a bit slower” on this sample can dominate the bill on terabytes. Check the physical plan with df.explain().







TipTakeaways




DataFrames = RDD + schema; the schema is what allows optimisation.
Filters can be written as pandas-style indexing, where/filter or SQL: same plan, so pick the most readable.
Nested data → select + withColumn + drop to flatten.
Prefer native column functions > pandas UDFs > Python UDFs.
Aggregate on the cluster, then toPandas() or histogram only the small result.

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
text: 18.1 The idea behind it

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
text:
Batch vs stream. Batch processing has all the data at the start; streaming processes unbounded data as it arrives, with low latency. Many real systems need both: a stream for fresh results, plus batch jobs that reprocess history (Real-time analytics).
Micro-batching. Spark turns a stream into a sequence of small batch jobs (one per trigger). You reuse the whole batch engine, at the price of latency of the order of the trigger interval, which is fine for most monitoring, not for microsecond trading.
State and fault tolerance. Aggregations over a stream must remember past batches (running counts). That state, plus the position in the input, has to survive crashes, which is what checkpoints and replayable sources are for. The TCP socket used here is not replayable, which is why Spark calls it test-only.

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
section: 18.2 The model: a stream is a table that keeps growing
text:
18.2 The model: a stream is a table that keeps growing
Structured Streaming lets you write the same DataFrame code as in Spark 2, and Spark runs it repeatedly on new data.


New records are appended as new rows of an (unbounded) input table.
Every trigger (e.g. every 2 s) processes the new rows as a micro-batch and updates a result table.
An output mode decides what is written to the sink each time.


Spark never stores the whole input table: each micro-batch is processed and dropped, and only the state needed for the result (e.g. running counts) is kept.








Output mode
Writes each trigger
Allowed for




append
only new result rows
queries without aggregation


update
only result rows that changed
most queries; used in this lab


complete
the whole result table
aggregations only



The overall pattern is source → transformations → sink. This lab uses a TCP socket as source and the console as sink; the Kafka lab replaces both with Kafka. Reading, cleaning and writing a stream continuously is called a real-time ETL pipeline (Extract, Transform, Load).
(The older RDD-based Spark Streaming, with DStreams, is deprecated; ignore it.)

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
text:
18.3 Session
Same as before, plus settings that keep streaming demos predictable on a tiny cluster:
.config("spark.sql.streaming.forceDeleteTempCheckpointLocation", "true")
.config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
...
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")       # otherwise the console sink is buried in logs

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
section: 18.4 The source: a socket and a producer
text:
18.4 The source: a socket and a producer
producer.py opens a server socket on spark-master:5555, waits for one client to connect, then sends a JSON line every 0.2 s:
{"name": "Jill", "surname": "Millers", "amount": 736.56, "delta_t": 7.78, "flag": 0}
flag is 1 with probability 0.2 (a “suspicious” transaction). Read the script before running it, since it is short.
It must run inside the cluster network, so start it in the master container:
cd code/spark
docker compose exec spark-master bash
python /mapd-workspace/notebooks/utils/producer.py --hostname spark-master
It exits when the streaming query disconnects, so restart the producer before every new query.






ImportantWhere is the output?



The console sink prints on the driver’s stdout, i.e. in the Jupyter container’s log, not in the notebook cell. Follow it with docker compose logs -f jupyter-notebook. The cell that calls .start() returns immediately: the query keeps running in the background until query.stop().

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
section: 18.5 First query: raw lines to the console
text:
18.5 First query: raw lines to the console
raw = (spark.readStream.format("socket")
            .option("host", "spark-master").option("port", 5555).load())

query = (raw.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("console")
            .trigger(processingTime='2 seconds').option("truncate", False).start())
# ... watch the log ...
query.stop()
Note the symmetry with batch code: read → readStream, write → writeStream. Spark warns that the socket source is for testing only, because it cannot replay data after a failure.
raw has a single string column value: Spark knows nothing about the JSON inside it yet.

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
section: 18.6 Develop on static data, then go live
text:
18.6 Develop on static data, then go live
Debugging a stream is painful, so the notebook first builds the parsing on a static DataFrame with the same shape (one string column of JSON lines):
from pyspark.sql.types import StringType, StructType, StructField, DoubleType, IntegerType
import pyspark.sql.functions as f

testDf = spark.createDataFrame(testData, StringType())

schema = StructType([StructField("name", StringType()), StructField("surname", StringType()),
                     StructField("amount", DoubleType()), StructField("delta_t", DoubleType()),
                     StructField("flag", IntegerType())])

parsed = testDf.select(f.from_json('value', schema=schema).alias('data')).select('data.*')
parsed.show()
from_json turns the string into one nested struct column; .alias('data') names it, and select('data.*') flattens it into five columns (the same flattening idea as in Spark 2).
Once it works, the identical code runs on the stream: swap testDf for raw. This is the main selling point of Structured Streaming.

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
text:
18.7 The fraud detector
Per micro-batch: count flagged transactions per user, and report users with more than one.
numTransactions = (parsed.where(f.col('flag') == 1)
                         .withColumn('id', f.concat(f.col('name'), f.col('surname')))
                         .groupBy('id').count())

susTransactions = (numTransactions.where(f.col('count') > 1)
                                  .withColumn('fraud', f.lit(1))        # constant column
                                  .select('id', 'fraud', f.col('count').alias('nTransactions')))

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 4)   # default is 200: far too many for this cluster

query = (susTransactions.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("console")
                        .trigger(processingTime='5 seconds').option("truncate", False).start())
Two things to notice:

groupBy in a stream is stateful: counts accumulate across batches (Spark keeps the running state). In update mode you see only the users whose count changed in the last trigger.
Re-run with outputMode("complete"): now every trigger prints the whole table. complete is only allowed because the query aggregates.

The shuffle.partitions line matters: the groupBy shuffles into 200 partitions by default, which means 200 tiny tasks per micro-batch on a 1–2 core cluster, and each trigger becomes very slow.

title: 18  Lab: Spark 3, Structured Streaming
text:
18.8 On a real system

The source would be a durable, replayable log, almost always Kafka (see the Kafka lab), so that after a crash Spark can re-read from the last checkpointed offset.
The sink would be a database, files in object storage, or another Kafka topic, not the console. Always set .option("checkpointLocation", "<reliable storage path>").
Unbounded state (like the per-user counts here, which grow forever) is controlled with event-time windows and watermarks: withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes").groupBy(window("ts", "5 minutes"), "id"), which lets Spark drop state for windows that can no longer change.
Streaming jobs run for days or months, so they are deployed with spark-submit and monitored (input rate vs processing rate: if processing is slower, the lag grows without bound).







TipTakeaways




A stream is a growing table; the query is ordinary DataFrame code, executed per micro-batch.
Develop on a static sample with the same schema, then switch the source.
Output modes: append (new rows), update (changed rows), complete (everything; aggregations only).
Aggregations are stateful across batches.
Console output goes to the driver log; queries run until stop().

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text: 19.1 The idea behind it
crumbs: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
Task graphs are the common language of parallel computing. Spark’s DAG, Dask’s graph and a Makefile are the same idea: nodes are pieces of work, edges are dependencies, and anything without a path between them can run in parallel. The scheduler’s job is to find that parallelism and place tasks on workers.
Granularity. Every task has a fixed cost (scheduling, serialisation, network: ~100 µs–1 ms in Dask). Parallelism helps only when each task’s work is much larger than that. Most of this lab’s exercises are deliberately too fine-grained, so you can see the overhead win.
Lazy vs eager are two styles of the same machinery: build the whole plan and let the scheduler optimise it (delayed), or start work immediately and keep results remote (futures), the way a batch system or a job queue behaves.
crumbs: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.2 Before you start
cd code/dask
docker compose up --scale dask-worker=2







Tab
What it shows




localhost:1234
Jupyter


localhost:8787
Dask dashboard: task stream (one row per worker thread, one bar per task), progress, worker memory



Keep the Task Stream panel of the dashboard visible: it is the Dask equivalent of the Spark UI, and the clearest way to see whether tasks really run in parallel.
crumbs: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.3 Dask in one paragraph
Dask is a task scheduler written in Python. You describe work as a graph of Python function calls, and the scheduler sends the calls to workers, respecting dependencies. On top of that it offers collections (bags, arrays, DataFrames) that generate those graphs for you. The ideas are the ones from Spark: partition the data, plan before executing, run close to the data. The difference is that everything, including the scheduler, is Python.
from dask.distributed import Client
client = Client('dask-scheduler:8786')     # service name + scheduler port
client                                     # shows workers, cores, memory, dashboard link
crumbs: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.4 Lazy: delayed
Three toy functions that each sleep(1) stand in for “real work”:
x = increment(1); y = decrement(2); z = add(x, y)       # plain Python: ~3 s
Wrapping calls in delayed records them instead of running them:
from dask import delayed
x = delayed(increment)(1)
y = delayed(decrement)(2)
z = delayed(add)(x, y)       # instant: z is a *plan*, not a number
z.visualize()                # draws the graph (needs graphviz)
z.compute()                  # runs it: ~2 s
Why 2 s and not 3: the graph shows increment and decrement are independent, so they run in parallel, and add waits for both. Dask found the parallelism from the dependencies; you did not write any threading code.

delayed(f)(args) = “call f later”. You can also decorate a function with @dask.delayed.
.visualize(optimize_graph=True) shows the graph after Dask’s optimisations; for graphs this simple there is nothing to optimise.
.compute() is blocking: it returns when the result is back in the notebook.
crumbs: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.5 Eager: submit, map and futures
future = client.submit(increment, 1)    # starts running NOW on the cluster
future                                  # status: pending → finished
client.gather(future)                   # bring the result to the notebook
A future is a handle to a result that is being computed, or already exists, on a worker. Data stays there until you gather it. You can pass futures as arguments to further submits, and Dask wires up the dependency without moving data through the notebook:
x = client.submit(increment, 1)
y = client.submit(decrement, 2)
total = client.submit(add, x, y)        # depends on x and y, which may not be ready yet
client.gather(total)
client.map(f, list) submits f once per element, which is the natural way to run the same function over many inputs (a parameter scan, say).




delayed + compute
submit/map + gather




when it runs
when you call compute()
immediately


style
build a whole graph, then run it
fire tasks as you go


result
returned by compute()
stays on workers until gather()


analogy
Spark transformations + action
a batch system



wait(futures) blocks until futures are finished without moving results to the notebook; gather waits and transfers.

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.6 Exercises

1. Parallel for loop. For each element of [1..8]: add a random number, multiply by 10; then sum everything. Do it with delayed, with submit, and with map.


Solution. 
results = [delayed(mult_ten)(delayed(add_rand)(x)) for x in data]
total = delayed(sum)(results)
total.compute()

# eager, element by element
total = client.submit(sum, [client.submit(mult_ten, client.submit(add_rand, x)) for x in data])
# eager, with map
total = client.submit(sum, client.map(mult_ten, client.map(add_rand, data)))
client.gather(total)
The graph is 8 independent chains joined by one sum: a pure “map then reduce”.


2. Tree reduction. Sum a list pairwise (add sleeps 1 s) instead of left to right.


Solution. Keep the plain-Python pairwise loop and wrap only the call: pair_sum = delayed(add)(L[i], L[i+1]). The loop now only builds a binary tree of additions; L[0].compute() runs each level in parallel. 9 elements take \(\lceil\log_2 9\rceil = 4\) levels, so about 4 s, against ~11 s for the sequential loop (it makes 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 calls, padding odd levels with add(x, 0)). This is exactly how distributed reduce works.


3. Word count over ~8000 newsgroup documents.


Solution. 
total = delayed(sum)([delayed(count_words)(doc) for doc in dataset])   # lazy
total = client.submit(sum, client.map(count_words, dataset))           # eager
Compare the timings with the plain loop: the parallel versions are not faster. Counting words in one document takes microseconds, while scheduling a task takes hundreds of microseconds. Too many tiny tasks are the problem, and Dask bags (next lab) fix it by batching elements into partitions.


4. Fibonacci with delayed.


Solution. Each new element depends on the two previous ones, so the graph is a chain: result.visualize(rankdir="LR") shows no branch that could run in parallel. A delayed object can be indexed (fibonacci[i]) and that indexing becomes a task too. Dask gives no speed-up for inherently sequential algorithms.


5–6. Monte Carlo integral and π. One delayed (or submit) call per random point.


Solution. These run slower than plain Python, which is the point of the exercise. 1,000–10,000 tasks of a few microseconds each are dominated by scheduling overhead (each task costs ~100s of µs). The fix is coarser tasks: each task generates a chunk of points and returns a partial count.
With futures, random functions need pure=False:
futures = [client.submit(in_circle, pure=False) for _ in range(num_points)]
By default Dask assumes functions are pure (same inputs give the same output) and deduplicates identical calls by hashing them, so without pure=False all 10,000 calls collapse into one task and you get the same point 10,000 times.

title: 19  Lab: Dask 1, delayed and futures
text:
19.7 On a real cluster

The scheduler/worker split is the same; only the deployment changes: dask-kubernetes / Dask Gateway on a Kubernetes cluster, dask-jobqueue on a Slurm/PBS HPC cluster (each worker is a batch job), or a managed service such as Coiled.
Adaptive scaling (cluster.adapt(minimum=2, maximum=50)) adds workers when tasks queue up and releases them when idle, which matters when you pay per VM-hour.
The dashboard you used on :8787 is the main debugging tool in production too: idle workers mean too little parallelism, many tiny tasks mean too fine granularity, and red transfer bars mean too much data movement.
Futures are a good fit for parameter scans and simulations on HPC (thousands of independent runs), which is a very common scientific use of Dask.

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text: 20.1 The idea behind it

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
Partition-level parallelism fixes the overhead problem of Dask 1: one task processes a whole partition (thousands of records), so the per-task cost is amortised.
The shuffle is the expensive part of distributed computing. Any “group by key” needs records with the same key on the same worker, so data crosses the network. groupby moves all records; foldby (like Spark’s reduceByKey, Hadoop’s combiner) first reduces inside each partition and moves only small partial results. Associativity of the reduction is what makes that legal.
Schema-on-read. Semi-structured data (JSON, logs) has no schema until you impose one by parsing and flattening, which is the “T” of ETL.

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
20.2 What a bag is
A dask.bag is a partitioned, lazy list of arbitrary Python objects: the Dask counterpart of a Spark RDD. It is the right tool for data that is not a table yet: text lines, logs, nested JSON. It solves the overhead problem from Dask 1: a function is applied to a whole partition per task, not to one element per task.
import dask.bag as db
b = db.from_sequence(range(1, 11), npartitions=4)
b.take(3)                                   # peek: computes only what is needed
From files, with one element per line and compression detected from the extension:
lines = db.read_text('datasets/accounts_json/accounts.*.json.gz', files_per_partition=4)
Paths are relative to the notebook (/mapd-workspace/notebooks in the container).

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
20.3 Map, filter, fold
c = b.filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0).map(lambda x: x ** 2)   # lazy
c.visualize()                                              # one chain per partition
c.compute()                                                # [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]
The reduction is called fold, and it shows the two levels of a distributed reduce explicitly:
c.fold(binop=lambda acc, x: acc + x,      # reduce inside each partition
       combine=lambda a, b: a + b)        # combine the partial results
Partitions matter. Re-run with npartitions=3 and compare the graphs. One partition means no parallelism; thousands of tiny partitions bring the scheduling overhead back. Aim for “a few partitions per core, each comfortably fitting in memory”.

20.3.1 Broadcast: scatter
The Dask version of Spark’s broadcast variables: send a read-only object (a lookup table, model parameters) to every worker once, then pass the future to tasks:
lut = client.scatter({0: "a", 1: "b", 2: "c"}, broadcast=True)
client.gather(client.map(lambda x, lut: f"{x} {lut[x % 3]}", range(20), lut=lut))
Without broadcast=True a single object goes to one worker (a list is spread round-robin), and the other workers fetch it when a task needs it.

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
20.4 Exploring the accounts data
Each line is a JSON document: {"id": …, "name": …, "transactions": [{"transaction-id": …, "amount": …}, …]}.
import json
records = lines.map(json.loads)          # text → dicts
records.take(1)
The bag toolkit for nested data:



Method
Does




map(f)
apply f to each element


filter(f)
keep elements where f is true


pluck(key)
element[key] for each element (go one level deeper)


flatten()
a bag of lists → a bag of their items



Questions are answered as pipelines, building them up one step at a time with .take(…) to check each stage:
alice = records.filter(lambda r: r['name'] == 'Alice')

# average number of transactions per Alice account
alice.map(lambda r: len(r['transactions'])).mean().compute()

# average amount over all of Alice's transactions
alice.pluck('transactions').flatten().pluck('amount').mean().compute()

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
20.5 Per-key aggregation: groupby vs foldby
“How many accounts per name?” can be done in two ways.
groupby puts every element with the same key together, then you reduce each group:
records.groupby(lambda r: r['name']).starmap(lambda name, group: (name, len(group))).compute()
starmap unpacks the (key, group) tuples into two arguments. The cost is that all records move across the network so that each key’s records end up together (a full shuffle), only to be counted.
foldby reduces while grouping: each partition keeps a running value per key, and only those small partial results are combined:
from operator import add
records.foldby(key='name',
               binop=lambda count, _: count + 1, initial=0,   # inside each partition
               combine=add, combine_initial=0).compute()      # across partitions
It is the same idea as Spark’s reduceByKey/combineByKey. Time both versions in the notebook: foldby wins, and the gap grows with the data. binop(acc, element) folds an element into the accumulator; combine(acc1, acc2) merges two accumulators. For a count, the two are different functions, which is why foldby needs both.

Total transferred amount per name, with foldby.


Solution. Pre-compute each account’s total with map, then fold the totals:
def sum_amount(r):
    return {'name': r['name'], 'total': sum(t['amount'] for t in r['transactions'])}

records.map(sum_amount).foldby(key='name',
                               binop=lambda acc, r: acc + r['total'], initial=0,
                               combine=add, combine_initial=0).compute()

title: 20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
20  Lab: Dask 2, Bags
text:
20.7 On a real cluster

Bags read the same storage as everything else: db.read_text("s3://bucket/logs/*.json.gz") (with s3fs installed), with one or a few files per partition. Large single files can be split with blocksize=, but gzip files cannot be split (the whole file is one partition), which is a common real-world bottleneck; prefer splittable formats or many medium-sized files.
Typical production use is the ingestion stage: parse and clean raw logs/JSON with a bag, then to_dataframe() and write Parquet for the analysis stage.
Broadcasting (scatter(..., broadcast=True)) matters more at scale: sending a 100 MB lookup table with every one of 10,000 tasks is 1 TB of network traffic.







TipTakeaways




Bags = RDDs for Python: lazy, partitioned, for semi-structured data.
map / filter / pluck / flatten navigate nested records; build pipelines step by step with take.
Prefer foldby (reduce while grouping) over groupby (shuffle everything first).
Choose partitions deliberately: not 1, not thousands.
Clean with a bag, then to_dataframe() for tabular work.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text: 21.1 The idea behind it

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
Horizontal partitioning of tables. A large table is split by rows into chunks that each fit in one worker’s memory; operations that work row-by-row or per-chunk parallelise perfectly, and operations that need a global view (sorting, global positions) don’t.
The index as the partitioning key. Dask can track the min/max index of each partition (its divisions). With a sorted index, lookups and joins on it touch only the relevant partitions, while on any other column they need a shuffle. This is the same idea as partition pruning in Spark and sharding by key in NoSQL databases.
Common sub-expression sharing: merging graphs (dask.compute(a, b)) avoids recomputing shared steps, the same optimisation a SQL planner does.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
21.2 What a Dask DataFrame is
A Dask DataFrame is many pandas DataFrames, the partitions, split along the index (row-wise, i.e. horizontal partitioning) and spread over the workers. Every operation you call is translated into the same pandas operation on each partition, plus whatever is needed to combine the results. The API is almost the pandas one, but the costs are different, and the lab is mostly about learning those costs.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
21.3 Loading
In pandas, reading many files means a loop and pd.concat into one in-memory table. In Dask, a glob is enough:
import dask, dask.dataframe as dd
dask.config.set({'dataframe.query-planning': True})   # enable the query optimiser (default in recent Dask)

df = dd.read_csv('datasets/accounts_csv/accounts.*.csv')
len(df)       # triggers work: len() of every partition, then a sum
df            # structure only: columns, dtypes, npartitions
df = df.repartition(npartitions=8)
By default you get roughly one partition per file, which is often not what you want. The number of partitions is your responsibility, as in Dask 2.
Unlike Spark, Dask DataFrames historically did no query optimisation: you got exactly the operations you wrote, in that order. The newer query planner adds some (e.g. pushing column selections and filters down), which is why the notebook makes sure it is on.

21.3.1 Type inference pitfall
Dask infers dtypes from a sample at the start of the data, then enforces them on all partitions. In nycflights, CRSElapsedTime and TailNum look like integers in the first rows but are not later, so head() works and tail() (a different partition) fails.
Fix it by stating the types:
df = dd.read_csv('datasets/nycflights/*.csv',
                 dtype={'TailNum': str, 'CRSElapsedTime': float})
Alternatives are a larger sample= or assume_missing=True (treat integer columns as floats, so they may contain NaN), but explicit dtypes are the robust fix.
Building a date column from three columns also needs meta, which tells Dask the output type without computing anything:
df['Date'] = dd.to_datetime(df.rename(columns={'Year': 'year', 'Month': 'month', 'DayofMonth': 'day'})
                              [['year', 'month', 'day']],
                            meta=pd.Series(dtype="datetime64[ns]"))

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
21.4 Cheap and expensive operations
Cheap (each partition works alone, then small results are combined):
df.DepDelay.max().compute()
df[df.UniqueCarrier == 'UA'].ArrDelay.mean().compute()
df.groupby(['Origin', 'Dest']).AirTime.max().compute()
df.groupby(['Origin', 'Dest'])['AirTime'].aggregate(['mean', 'std']).compute()
df.loc[df['Dest'] == 'DEN', ['UniqueCarrier']].compute()



Task graph of max(): a max per partition, then a max of maxes.


Group-by aggregations are still reasonably fast: partial aggregates per partition, then a combine. The result lands in one partition; if it is large, split_out= spreads it.
Not available or expensive:







Operation
Why




df.iloc[0:10] (row positions)
raises: partitions don’t know their global row numbers. iloc[:, cols] (columns only) works


set_index(col)
needs a full sort of the data across workers


sort_values, joins on a non-index column
full shuffle


df.compute() on everything
brings all data to the client, so only after reducing it



The typical workflow is therefore: bag to clean the raw input, Dask DataFrame to filter and reduce the bulk, then pandas (.compute()) on the small result for anything order-dependent or fiddly.
After an unavoidable expensive step, persist the result so later operations don’t repeat it:
ua_den = df[(df.UniqueCarrier == 'UA') & (df.Dest == 'DEN')].set_index('Date')   # sort happens here
ua_den.ArrDelay.rolling('5D').mean().compute()     # time-based rolling needs the datetime index

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
section: 21.5 Share work: one dask.compute for several results
text:
21.5 Share work: one dask.compute for several results
df = df.persist()                      # keep the parsed data in worker memory (not in place!)
non_cancelled = df[df.Cancelled == 0]
mean_delay = non_cancelled.DepDelay.mean()
std_delay  = non_cancelled.DepDelay.std()

mean_delay.compute(); std_delay.compute()             # two graphs, common steps done twice
dask.compute(mean_delay, std_delay)                   # one merged graph: ~half the time



Merged graph: reading, filtering and the shared sums/counts are computed once and feed both results.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
section: 21.6 Exercise: the dimuon spectrum in Dask
text:
21.6 Exercise: the dimuon spectrum in Dask
The same analysis as Spark 2, built from the Dask pieces. The JSON files are already in code/dask/notebooks/datasets/dimuon in the fork; the notebook’s instruction to copy them over from spark/ is only needed on a fresh upstream checkout.

Read and parse with a bag: each file is one JSON array of events, so parse and flatten:
events = db.read_text('datasets/dimuon/*.json', files_per_partition=4).map(json.loads).flatten()
Events per sample with foldby (count per key, as in Dask 2):
events.foldby(key='sample', binop=lambda n, _: n + 1, initial=0, combine=add, combine_initial=0).compute()
Muon multiplicity per sample: filter on sample, pluck('nMuon'), compute(), histogram in matplotlib.
Select and flatten to a DataFrame: two muons, opposite charge, then one flat dict per event:
df = (events.filter(lambda e: e['nMuon'] == 2)
            .filter(lambda e: e['Muons'][0]['charge'] == -e['Muons'][1]['charge'])
            .map(flatten_records)          # {'sample', 'E1', 'px1', ..., 'pz2'}
            .to_dataframe())
Features are plain pandas-style column arithmetic (lazy):
df['pT1'] = np.sqrt(df.px1**2 + df.py1**2);  df['pT2'] = np.sqrt(df.px2**2 + df.py2**2)
df = df[(df.pT1 > 15) & (df.pT2 > 15)]
df['E'] = df.E1 + df.E2;  df['Px'] = df.px1 + df.px2  # ... Py, Pz
df['M'] = np.sqrt(df.E**2 - (df.Px**2 + df.Py**2 + df.Pz**2))
Reduce, then go to pandas for plotting: df[['sample', 'M', 'pT1', 'pT2']].compute().

Compared with Spark: no UDF machinery, since numpy works directly on the columns because every partition is a pandas DataFrame.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
21.7 On a real cluster

Use Parquet on object storage: dd.read_parquet("s3://bucket/flights/", columns=[...], filters=[("Year", ">=", 2000)]) reads only the needed columns and row groups, and the stored schema removes the dtype-inference problem entirely.
Set the index once (expensive) and save the result partitioned by it, so later jobs get the divisions for free.
Size partitions to roughly 100 MB–1 GB in memory; check with df.memory_usage_per_partition().compute(). Workers that run out of memory spill to disk and slow down dramatically.
The “bag → Dask DataFrame → pandas” pattern is how most Python data platforms are built: distributed tools for the heavy reduction, single-machine tools for the final, small result.

title: 21  Lab: Dask 3, DataFrames
text:
21.8 Wrap up
client.close(), then docker compose down.






TipTakeaways




Dask DataFrame = row-wise partitions that are each a pandas DataFrame.
State dtypes explicitly; inference only looks at the beginning of the data.
Per-partition operations and group-by aggregations are cheap; iloc, set_index, sorting and non-index joins are not.
persist after expensive steps; compute related results together with dask.compute(...).
Bag (clean) → Dask DataFrame (reduce) → pandas (finish).

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text: 22.1 The idea behind it
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
Decoupling with a log. Producers and consumers never know about each other; the broker stores an ordered, durable log in between. New consumers can be added later and replay history, and a slow consumer does not slow down producers. This is the backbone of event-driven architectures.
Partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering, as in Spark: more partitions allow more consumers in parallel, and order is guaranteed only inside one partition. The key decides the partition, so you choose the key for the ordering you need (e.g. per user).
Replication for fault tolerance. Each partition has a leader and followers on other brokers (theory). This lab uses one broker, so replication_factor=1, i.e. no fault tolerance at all.
Delivery semantics. At-most-once, at-least-once or exactly-once depend on when offsets are committed relative to processing, and on whether writes are idempotent.
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
22.2 Before you start
cd code/kafka
docker compose up --scale spark-worker=2     # the README advises at most 2 workers
The broker is reachable inside the Docker network as kafka-broker:9092; it is not published to your laptop, so everything (shell tools, Python clients, Spark) runs in a container.
Notebook 1 installs the client library with !pip install kafka-python. It lives in the container, so you need to repeat it after every docker compose down.
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
22.3 Kafka in one picture
Kafka is a log, not a queue. A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an append-only, ordered list of records, and each record gets a position, the offset. Producers append to the end. Consumers read from wherever they like and remember their offset. Reading does not delete anything, so many independent consumers can read the same data, at different speeds, now or later. Producers and consumers never talk to each other, only to the broker. That decoupling is the whole point.
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
section: 22.4 Part 1: from the shell (on the broker)
text:
22.4 Part 1: from the shell (on the broker)
docker compose exec kafka-broker bash
cd $KAFKA_HOME/bin
./kafka-topics.sh --list     --bootstrap-server kafka-broker:9092
./kafka-topics.sh --create   --topic my_awesome_topic --bootstrap-server kafka-broker:9092
./kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic my_awesome_topic --bootstrap-server kafka-broker:9092
Then open two shells on the broker, one for each side:
./kafka-console-producer.sh --topic my_awesome_topic --bootstrap-server kafka-broker:9092
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic my_awesome_topic --bootstrap-server kafka-broker:9092 --from-beginning
Type in the producer and lines appear in the consumer. Start the consumer without --from-beginning and it only shows new messages; with it, it replays everything. The data was kept even though nobody was reading.
--bootstrap-server is just an entry point: the client asks that broker for the cluster layout, then talks to whichever broker leads each partition.
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
22.5 Part 2: producing from Python (Producer.ipynb)
from kafka import KafkaProducer
producer = KafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers=['kafka-broker:9092'])

producer.send('my_awesome_topic', b'message 1')    # returns a future: queued, NOT sent yet
producer.flush()                                   # force the queue out now
send is asynchronous: messages are buffered and sent in batches, which is how Kafka reaches high throughput. If a script exits right after send without flush() (or close()), the messages may never leave. Values (and keys) are bytes: you choose the serialisation, e.g. json.dumps(d).encode().
Close the producer and create a new one: the topic and its messages are unaffected, because producers are disposable.
Keys. producer.send(topic, key=b'user42', value=...). The key is hashed to choose the partition, so all messages with the same key go to the same partition, in order. Without a key, the producer spreads messages over partitions.
Admin API. Creating topics from Python, with a chosen number of partitions:
from kafka.admin import KafkaAdminClient, NewTopic
admin = KafkaAdminClient(bootstrap_servers=['kafka-broker:9092'])
admin.create_topics([NewTopic(name='a_partitioned_topic', num_partitions=2, replication_factor=1)])
admin.list_topics()
replication_factor=1 because there is a single broker; on a real cluster you would use 3. The notebook ends by sending 20 fake transactions (the JSON from the Spark streaming lab) to a_partitioned_topic, and creating a results topic for later.
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
22.6 Part 3: consuming (Consumer.ipynb)
from kafka import KafkaConsumer
consumer = KafkaConsumer(bootstrap_servers=['kafka-broker:9092'],
                         consumer_timeout_ms=10000)   # stop iterating after 10 s without messages
consumer.subscribe(['my_awesome_topic'])
for msg in consumer:                                   # polls the broker
    print(msg.partition, msg.offset, msg.key, msg.value)
Without consumer_timeout_ms the for loop never ends (a consumer waits for new data forever), so interrupt the kernel to stop it.
Each record carries its partition, offset, timestamp, key and value. consumer.seek_to_beginning() moves the offset back to 0 and the topic is read again, the Python version of --from-beginning.
On a_partitioned_topic you see messages from partitions 0 and 1 interleaved: order is guaranteed only within a partition, never across the topic.
Reading one partition only. Instead of subscribe (let Kafka decide), assign picks partitions by hand:
from kafka import TopicPartition
c0 = KafkaConsumer(bootstrap_servers=['kafka-broker:9092'], consumer_timeout_ms=10000)
c0.assign([TopicPartition('a_partitioned_topic', 0)])
c0.seek_to_beginning()
crumbs: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
text:
22.7 Part 4: consumer groups (Consumer.ipynb + ConsumerGroup.ipynb)
Consumers that share a group_id split the partitions of a topic between them: each partition is read by exactly one member of the group. This is how Kafka scales reading.
consumer_one = KafkaConsumer(bootstrap_servers=['kafka-broker:9092'],
                             client_id='consumer_one', group_id='my_group',
                             auto_offset_reset='earliest', consumer_timeout_ms=10000)
consumer_one.subscribe(['a_partitioned_topic'])
Create consumer_two with the same group_id in ConsumerGroup.ipynb, then run both read loops at the same time (they are separate kernels, i.e. separate processes):

consumer_one.assignment() and consumer_two.assignment() show one partition each: the group rebalanced.
Each prints only its partition’s messages.
Stop one, and after a rebalance the other takes over both partitions.
A consumer in a different group would get all messages again: groups are independent readers.

auto_offset_reset='earliest' applies only when the group has no stored offset yet (start from the beginning instead of only new messages). Afterwards the group’s committed offsets win, so a second run continues where the group stopped.

title: 22  Lab: Kafka, and Kafka + Spark
section: 22.8 Part 5: Kafka as Spark source and sink (KafkaSpark_StructuredStreaming.ipynb)
text:
22.8 Part 5: Kafka as Spark source and sink (KafkaSpark_StructuredStreaming.ipynb)
The fraud detector from Spark 3, with the socket replaced by Kafka on both ends:
Producer.ipynb ──► topic a_partitioned_topic ──► Spark (parse, count flags per user) ──► topic results ──► Consumer.ipynb
The Kafka connector is not part of core Spark; it is downloaded when the session starts:
.config("spark.jars.packages", "org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.1.1")
.config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 4)
Source. Same readStream, different format:
raw = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
            .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka-broker:9092")
            .option("subscribe", "a_partitioned_topic")
            .option("startingOffsets", "latest")      # only messages arriving from now on
            .load())
raw.printSchema()    # key, value (binary), topic, partition, offset, timestamp, ...
Kafka rows are binary key/value plus metadata, so the value is cast to string before parsing the JSON:
parsed = raw.select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("data")).select("data.*")
Because of startingOffsets = latest, re-run the sending cell in Producer.ipynb after starting the query, or you will see nothing. The console output appears in the Jupyter container log, as in Spark 3.
Transform. Identical to Spark 3, except that the output must look like a Kafka record: a key and a value column, both strings or bytes:
sus = (parsed.where(col('flag') == 1)
             .withColumn('id', concat(col('name'), col('surname')))
             .groupBy('id').count().where(col('count') > 1)
             .withColumn('fraud', lit(1))
             .select(col('id').alias('key'), col('fraud').cast(StringType()).alias('value')))
Sink.
query = (sus.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("kafka")
            .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka-broker:9092")
            .option("topic", "results")
            .option("checkpointLocation", "checkpoint")   # required for the Kafka sink
            .start())
The checkpoint directory is where Spark records which input offsets it has processed and its aggregation state, so a restarted query continues instead of starting over. It is created in the notebooks folder; delete it to start from scratch.
Finally, the last section of Consumer.ipynb subscribes to results and prints an “alert” for each flagged user: a third, independent application reacting to Spark’s output. For end-to-end exactly-once behaviour you would also need idempotent or transactional writes on the sink side (see the theory); this lab’s pipeline is at-least-once.

22.9 On a real cluster

At least 3 brokers, topics with replication_factor=3, and producers with acks="all" (a write is confirmed only once in-sync replicas have it), together with min.insync.replicas=2. This configuration survives losing a broker without losing data.
Security: the commented-out producer/consumer examples in the notebooks (security_protocol="SSL", ssl_cafile=...) are what a real cluster looks like: TLS plus client certificates or SASL credentials.
Retention: logs are deleted after a time or size limit (retention.ms), or compacted to keep the last value per key. Kafka is a buffer and a history, not a permanent archive.
Consumer lag (latest offset − committed offset per partition) is the key health metric: if it grows, consumers can’t keep up, so add consumers (up to the number of partitions) or partitions.
Managed Kafka (AWS MSK, Confluent Cloud) handles brokers and upgrades; the client code is the same as in the notebooks, with different bootstrap_servers and credentials.

query.stop(), spark.stop(), then docker compose down.






TipTakeaways




A topic is a set of append-only, partitioned logs; reading does not consume, and consumers track offsets.
send is asynchronous: flush() before exiting.
Same key → same partition → ordered; no global order across partitions.
Within a group, partitions are shared out (scaling); across groups, everyone gets everything (fan-out).
Spark reads Kafka with readStream.format("kafka") and writes back with key/value columns and a checkpoint.
